title: Carrier-is-memory: the mandatory carrier wafer of backside-power logic becomes a DRAM wafer
idea: In backside power delivery the finished front-side BEOL is flipped and bonded to a carrier wafer, the original substrate is ground away and power is wired in from the back, so the front-side signal wiring ends up facing the carrier. Replace that blank carrier with a full DRAM wafer (1-beta-class 1T1C or an oxide-cell wafer) whose die map matches the logic reticle, and make the bond a Cu-SiCN hybrid bond at 1-2 um pitch instead of a plain dielectric fusion bond. The memory die keeps its sense amps and bank logic but drops pads, PHYs and TSVs; commands, data and memory power cross the bond. The memory wafer stays thick and becomes the heat-spreading side of the stack (pair with B3-03). For a wafer-scale engine, the same move puts a whole 300 mm DRAM wafer (~3.9 TB) under the compute wafer.
why: Memory interface energy ~12x lower (3.5 -> ~0.28 pJ/bit), saving ~200-410 W per accelerator at 8-16 TB/s; 45-53 GB per 800 mm2 logic die with zero added footprint and no HBM stacking; ~$1.7-2.3/GB of added memory at DRAM-wafer cost.
note: Backside-power carrier wafer is mandatory anyway; making it DRAM gives ~12x lower interface energy at zero footprint. Doubt: logic-DRAM die-map and yield coupling.

title: Cochlear amplifier: Hopf-poised sense amp hears sub-femtofarad cells
idea: Cochlear hair cells sit at a Hopf bifurcation, giving huge gain for faint sounds; bias each sense amplifier at the edge of oscillation with a calibrated negative-resistance loop so the tiny bitline perturbation of a ~1 fF cell tips it decisively, with per-amp calibration of the bifurcation point.
why: Capacitor charge wall: if 1-2 fF cells become readable, pillar AR can fall from 60-75:1 to ~15-20:1, cutting deposition/etch cost and opening lateral 3D capacitors.
note: Latches already regenerate from instability; Hopf poise does not beat kT/C noise or offset.

title: Ink-saver encoding keeps fewest cells in leaky charged state
idea: Like ink-saving fonts that print letters with holes, encode each burst with a low-weight code (e.g., 16b to 18b with per-group inversion) chosen using the die's true-cell/anti-cell map, so as few cells as possible sit in the charged state that leaks; retention failures are nearly all charged-to-discharged.
why: Cuts the population of retention-vulnerable cells by ~30-40%, so the same leakage tail (fact 3) yields fewer failures and refresh can stretch ~1.5x; restore energy drops slightly (fact 10) for ~6-12% capacity cost.

title: CDN edge caching: weak memory tier holds only clean data
idea: Adapted from CDNs, which can lose a cached object because the origin always has a copy: the OS places only clean, file-backed pages (page cache, read-only model files, container images) on a pool of cheap low-grade DRAM with detection-only codes, and any detected error simply invalidates the page and refetches it from SSD.
why: Cost per bit (facts 3, 4): page cache is often 30-60% of server memory; serving it from salvaged or relaxed-spec DRAM frees premium DRAM for dirty data, and an error costs a ~50 us refetch instead of a crash.

title: Chilled-DIMM certification grade with 256 ms refresh
idea: Worse: run DRAM at 85-95 C, where leakage doubles every ~10 C. Flip: create a 'cold-loop' grade: modules on datacenter liquid cold plates held at 25-35 C are binned and certified for 256 ms refresh, and dies that fail the hot spec but pass cold are sold into this grade.
why: Fact 3 and yield: 4x less refresh and a new outlet for retention-weak dies that would otherwise be scrapped; rides on the liquid cooling already arriving with AI racks.

title: Data-parallel training: model replicas become each other's ECC
idea: In a 10,000-GPU job, every data-parallel rank holds identical weights. Periodically checksum each 2 MB weight shard, compare checksums across replicas over NVLink or InfiniBand, and repair any mismatched shard by copying it from a majority peer. Local HBM errors are then corrected by replication that already exists.
why: Weights are ~30-50% of training HBM. Cross-replica voting gives TMR-like protection for free and lets weight regions run on weaker dies or relaxed refresh (facts 3, 6).

title: Aviation dissimilar redundancy: cross-vendor ECC words
idea: Adapted from fly-by-wire systems that use dissimilar processors from different vendors so one design flaw cannot fail every channel: each ECC codeword in a module or CXL pool is assembled from dies of at least three different vendors or process lots, so a vendor-specific weakness (a hammer-sensitive layout, a lot-wide retention excursion) can hit only one symbol.
why: Row hammer and correlated failures (facts 3, 9): chipkill assumes independent dies, but real failures cluster by vendor and lot; dissimilar assembly makes existing ECC far stronger in practice and lets riskier lower-bin parts fill each slot.
note: Dissimilar-lot codeword assembly decorrelates failures; proof needs fleet failure data.

title: Selective-assembly die pairing matches complementary defect maps
idea: Bearing makers measure parts and mate oversized balls with undersized races; record each die's failing and weak-row map at wafer test and pair dies into stacks or ranks whose bad addresses do not overlap, so cheap module-level mirroring or spare sharing covers one die's holes with its partner's good rows.
why: Rescues dies that exceed on-die redundancy (several yield points) and makes cross-die repair nearly free because overlaps are engineered to near zero.

title: Decommissioned-server DRAM recertified by in-system retention retest
idea: Combine e-waste recycling with in-system profiling: retired DDR4/DDR5 modules pass through an automated rack that runs retention and hammer profiling, writes per-module weak-row maps into SPD and redeploys them behind stronger controller ECC as CXL-attached expansion.
why: Supply shortage: reclaims existing bits with no fab capital and US-located refurbishment, delivering usable memory at a fraction of new price.

title: Second-life DRAM: re-certify decommissioned server dies under strong ECC
idea: Worse: shred millions of 3-5 year old DIMMs while new bits cost 4x more. Flip: industrial lines recover modules from retired servers, run deep retention and hammer profiling, and resell them graded into tiers behind controllers with chipkill plus elastic refresh for cold or secondary memory pools.
why: Supply and scarce resources: part of the installed base (tens of exabytes) could return as CXL capacity tiers using zero new wafers.

title: Grade-B DRAM exchange selling dies with certified error maps
idea: Box [medium: any | access: any | sense: standard | integration: DIMM or CXL | substrate: bulk | fab: existing fabs]. A broker buys dies that fail JEDEC retention or hammer limits, tests each to a signed per-die error map, and sells them to hyperscalers whose controllers load the map to retire rows and set per-bank refresh.
why: Supply: unlocks the 5-15% of output that is scrapped or downbinned today, at ~40% discount.

title: Epidemic contact tracing: ECC events trigger blast-radius refresh
idea: Epidemiologists trace and test the contacts of each case. When row r reports a corrected error, controller firmware treats it as a case. It immediately refreshes and scrubs r+-1..+-4 using the physical adjacency map. If more cases appear, it raises local refresh and asks the OS to quarantine (remap) the hot aggressor pages.
why: Free ECC events become hammer and weak-cell sensors (facts 3 and 9), and stop cascades before they reach uncorrectable errors. It needs firmware and a kernel hook only.
